messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 65
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 65

He is 65 now, a career prosecutor who has spent decades standing in courtrooms, arranging facts into timelines, asking juries to trust evidence over emotion. For most of his adult life, he believes in institutions, even when they are imperfect. He believes in procedure, in records, in the idea that if something wrong happens, there is a way to name it and answer for it. That faith is what makes the night of the assault so difficult to place in his own mind, because it is not only frightening; it feels like a betrayal of the rules by the very people meant to enforce them.

It happens four years ago, after he leaves his office later than usual. He is still in a suit, carrying a worn leather briefcase, thinking about a witness problem in an upcoming case. A block from where he parked, he sees flashing lights and an argument spilling onto the sidewalk. He slows but keeps walking, wanting no part of it. One officer turns suddenly, shouts something he does not fully catch, and before he can orient himself, he is ordered to get on the ground. He tries to explain who he is, even reaches toward his inside pocket for identification. That movement changes everything. He is slammed against a car, then onto the pavement. A knee drives into his back. His cheek grinds into oil and grit. He remembers the strange clarity of seeing a crushed cigarette near his face while someone yells that he is resisting. He is not resisting. He is 61 years old, winded, confused, saying, “I’m a prosecutor. My badge is in my wallet,” and hearing his own voice sound thin and unreal.

He is handcuffed hard enough that his wrists bruise for days. Someone strikes him near the ribs. Another officer curses at him, calls him a liar. The worst part, he says later, is not the pain but the instant certainty that nothing he says matters. For several minutes, his life is in other people’s hands, and those hands are careless. When a supervisor finally arrives and recognizes his name, the mood shifts almost theatrically. He is lifted up, uncuffed, addressed as “sir.” There are apologies, then explanations, then a suggestion that everyone has had a stressful night. He goes home with torn trousers, shallow breathing, and a metallic taste in his mouth that lingers long after the blood is gone.

At first he treats it like an incident to document. He photographs the bruises. He dictates notes into his phone. He tells his wife in a controlled, clipped voice, as if presenting a case. But over the next weeks, the order he tries to impose on it slips. He cannot sleep for more than an hour or two at a time. He jolts awake with his heart racing, back muscles rigid, convinced for a moment that someone is on top of him. If headlights sweep across the bedroom ceiling, his body reacts before his mind does. His wife reaches toward him in the dark and he flinches.

He starts avoiding the street where it happened, then the whole downtown area after sunset. He tells colleagues he prefers remote meetings because they are efficient, but really he cannot bear walking past cruisers parked outside the courthouse. The sight of uniforms now produces a pulse of heat and dread that embarrasses him. In court he remains polished, but he notices himself tracking every officer in the room, watching belts, hands, stance, tone. When police witnesses testify, he becomes unusually rigid. Small inconsistencies that once seemed routine now ignite anger out of proportion to the moment. He hears himself speaking sharply, almost contemptuously, and afterward feels ashamed.

At home he is less patient than he used to be. He startles at the slam of the garbage truck, at sirens, at his grandson running up behind him in the yard. He used to take evening walks with his wife; now he checks the locks twice and says he is too tired. She tells him he seems far away even when he is sitting beside her. He knows what she means. Whole stretches of the day feel narrowed, as if his attention is always partly occupied by a threat no one else can see. He no longer reads crime novels, though he once loved them. News stories about misconduct pull him in and leave him shaking. He tells himself he should be able to think clearly about these things—this is his profession, after all—but his body does not care about his profession.

What troubles him most is how the event has altered his sense of himself. He has spent a lifetime presenting as composed, rational, hard to rattle. Now he studies parking lots before getting out of the car. He keeps his wallet visible in his hand if he sees police nearby. He rehearses sentences in advance: “My name is—,” “I am reaching slowly—,” “My identification is here.” He hates that he does this. He hates even more that it feels necessary.

He still goes to work. He still prepares cases meticulously and stands when the judge enters and speaks in the steady voice people expect from him. But underneath that practiced control, he carries the memory in his muscles: pavement against his face, the weight on his back, the impossibility of making himself understood. For him, the worst injury is not only fear. It is that the world he organized his life around no longer feels reliably governed by the rules he served.
